item.title: Magic of Dicke states: density, cost and yield
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — The stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) of Dicke states is extensive at all fillings f=n/L∈(0,1) except f=1/2, following M2(|DnL⟩)=Lα(f)+2log2⁡L+c(f)+o(1). Average distillable CCZ yield per qubit is non-zero and extensive across all 0<f<1, equalling 12f(1−f)[(1−f)4+f4] despite M2 scaling only as 2log2⁡(πL/8)−1 at f=1/2.

Grade 0.417 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Yves H. Kwan

Figure

Magic density per qubit and CCZ yield per qubit plotted versus excitation filling fraction f. It shows that SRE vanishes only at f=1/2 and the poles, whereas average CCZ extraction rate remains strictly positive across all non-trivial fillings.

Asks

How does the non-stabilizerness (magic) of Dicke states scale in the thermodynamic limit at fixed filling, and what is their resource yield for fault-tolerant quantum computing?

Before

SRE was known only for fixed small excitation count n (M2∼2nlog2⁡L) or at half-filling where M2≃2log2⁡(πL/8)−1 (large-L approximation by Oliviero et al. 2022).

But

Asymptotic thermodynamic limit L→∞ with fixed filling fraction f=n/L. Yields fluctuate by O(L) run-to-run (non-self-averaging) due to an emergent hidden phase.

Tools

Stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) · Magnetization projection of tilted-spin product states · Branch bound on magic · Heralded resource distillation protocols

Abstract

Dicke states are an elementary family of many-body quantum states, consisting of equal superpositions of all configurations of L qubits with n excitations. We show that their magic, as measured by the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE), is extensive at every filling f=n/L except half-filling, and we obtain the magic density analytically, together with the subleading terms. In the context of fault-tolerant quantum computation, we also investigate the yield of Dicke states, and find that they can produce on average an extensive number of CCZ states (or T states with a catalyst) at any 0<f<1. This yield is not self-averaging, but fluctuates from run to run by O(L), as if it were set by a hidden phase shared by all qubits. At half-filling, the SRE grows only logarithmically, while the preparation cost, average yield and relative entropy of magic remain extensive, so that a small SRE does not necessarily signal a weak resource. These results can be understood by viewing the Dicke state as a fixed-magnetization projection of a product of tilted spins.

item.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Agentic evolutionary program synthesis automatically finds fault-tolerant dynamic Clifford circuits for logical state preparation, logical gates, code switching, and code growth, verified by exhaustive fault evaluation.

Grade 0.416 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Aritra Lahiri, Florian Marquardt

Figure

The agentic evolutionary program synthesis workflow. Left: prompt specification with targets, layout, and fault-tolerance constraints. Right: LLM tool use, verifier evaluation, island-based database scoring, and inter-generation memory.

Asks

Can automated LLM-driven program evolution discover fault-tolerant quantum circuits across the full stack of logical operations?

Before

Automated discovery via satisfiability solving or RL was limited to distance-five codes, restricted to state preparation, and required orders of magnitude more circuit simulations.

But

Restricted to stabilizer/Clifford circuits and single-fault verification models (t=1 in reported traces).

Tools

agentic FunSearch · large language models · stabilizer tableau verification · dynamic Clifford circuits · island-based evolutionary search

Abstract

Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

item.title: Entropic quantum error correction for independent and correlated amplitude damping errors
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Non-global entropic recovery map yields entanglement fidelity FEnt=1−1.25t2+O(t3) and worst-case fidelity Fmin⁡2=1−1.25t2+O(t3) for independent amplitude damping, computed using only 2×2 unitaries.

Grade 0.416 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Gang Zhou

Asks

Can quantum conditional mutual information guide the construction of an explicit, non-global, computationally inexpensive quantum error correction recovery map for independent and correlated amplitude damping noise?

Before

For independent errors, Petz-map recovery achieved FEnt=1−1.25γ2+O(γ3) and Fmin⁡2=1−1.15γ2+O(γ3) (Biswas & Mandayam 2021).

But

Short codeword length (n=4), damping parameter t≪1 (perturbation expansion up to O(t2)), speed of light assumed c=∞ in the field model.

Tools

quantum conditional mutual information · four-qubit Leung code · operator convexity · non-global error recovery maps

Abstract

The idea of using quantum entropy for quantum error correction (QEC) has existed for a long time. However, its computational complexity has limited its practical use: even a [[4,1]] code for standard independent amplitude damping errors involves a 256×256 Hermitian matrix, so the approach scales poorly as the codeword length increases. For correlated errors, the situation is even worse. In this paper, we show that, by using the insights developed in our previous paper and exploiting certain structures of quantum conditional mutual information, we can solve these problems exactly by hand, using only 2×2 unitary matrices. By examining the entropy, we identify the leakage channels and the amount of leakage exactly, then define the recovery map accordingly. The rules defining our recovery map are simple, intuitive, and computationally inexpensive: for independent errors, it is based on 16 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions; for correlated errors, it is based on 6 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions. Our method sacrifices little in terms of performance: for the widely used entanglement fidelity, our simple QEC recovery map achieves a sharp result; for the worst-case fidelity, the best result is about 9% better than ours; for correlated errors, there are no comparable results for short codewords. Among the known techniques, our recovery map is the first non-global one. The calculations use elementary linear algebra and calculus, and is presented in great detail.

item.title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Encodes and decodes up to 1568 real classical values across entire quantum processors without SWAP gates or ancilla qubits by 2-colouring bipartite coupling graphs into shared address and data qubits.

Grade 0.413 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Daniel Bultrini

Figure

Reconstruction of 784-pixel grayscale and 1568-value colour pixel art retrieved experimentally from IBM Phoenix using 8192 shots per basis with and without phase encoding.

Asks

How can classical data be parallel-encoded across a quantum processor without SWAP routing overhead or ancilla qubits under limited hardware connectivity?

Before

QPIXL and QCrank required star connectivity between all address and data registers, forcing SWAP routing on planar hardware.

But

Requires bipartite coupling subgraphs; error rate grows with local qubit degree and state density, requiring 8192–32768 readout shots per basis.

Tools

multiplexer compiling · bipartite graph 2-colouring · scaled fast Walsh–Hadamard transform · IBM Phoenix · IBM Fez

Abstract

We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to 1568 real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data. Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits. When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree. As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.

item.title: Local gluing classification and bulk-locked clock rings for Z_N models on a Klein bottle
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Local commuting reflection gluings in the ℤN plaquette model form a family indexed by units u∈ℤN×. Gluings exist for all N at even seam length Lx, and at odd Lx if and only if −1 is a quadratic residue modulo N.

Grade 0.377 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Junhao (Eigen), Wang

Figure

Lattice layout of the mirror Klein bottle in the site register showing the identification of virtual row Ly with row 0 and far-corner placements of seam plaquettes.

Asks

Which local reflection gluings of the ℤN plaquette model on a Klein bottle yield commuting check algebras, and what spectrum results from the obstructed literal seam?

But

Restricted to local monomial far-corner gluings of the standard bulk plaquette model. No non-stabilizer resources generated within static Clifford/Weyl operations 𝒪.

Tools

monomial far-corner ansatz · Howell and Smith normal forms · Lanczos exact diagonalization · twisted homology

Abstract

We classify local reflection gluings of the Z_N plaquette model on lattice Klein bottles and solve the obstructed literal seam. Within the monomial far-corner ansatz, all commuting gluings form a family labelled by a unit u of Z_N. They exist for every N at even seam length and, at odd length, exactly when -1 is a square modulo N. We determine the anyon transport, including exchange seams with P²=C for charge conjugation C, and the relation phases that distinguish an unfrustrated code from a commuting but frustrated Hamiltonian. For the literal gluing, the 2L_x noncommuting plaquettes form self-dual clock rings whose sectors are locked by the bulk. This gives an exact reduction of the spectrum to clock-ring spectra, closed-form ring ground energies for N=2,4, and a closed-form ground-state degeneracy. We further determine twisted-coefficient homology on the stated surface domains and compare it with logical modules on registered lattice grids; composite dimensions need not give squares of cyclic groups. Dressed-isometry gates and monodromy are reported with their finite-grid scope. Finally, the qudit Gottesman--Knill theorem bounds the computational interpretation: Clifford deformations and Weyl measurements with stabilizer inputs and no external magic states cannot supply a non-stabilizer resource. Charge-conjugation measurements that do supply such states lie outside this operation model. The new results concern explicit seam classification, phase-sensitive consistency and bulk-locked spectra, not a new general no-go theorem or a universal computing architecture.

item.title: Efficient quantum-circuit simulation of classical control of computational order
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Any transformation with classical control of computational order on N independent channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated by fixed-order quantum circuits using at most N2 queries, or catalytically without consuming the extra N2−N queries.

Grade 0.375 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Raphaël Mothe, Jessica Bavaresco

Asks

Can quantum processes with dynamical or indefinite causal order be efficiently simulated by standard quantum circuits with fixed causal order?

But

Restricted to unitary input channels (non-universal) when extending to quantum control of computational order.

Tools

classical control of causal order · query complexity analysis · catalytic simulation · quantum instruments · fixed-order quantum circuits

Abstract

We show that quantum circuits with classical control of computational order admit an efficient simulation by fixed-order quantum circuits: any such transformation acting on N independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated using at most N² queries. We generalize these constructions to extended, bipartite quantum channels and quantum instruments, and demonstrate that they can be implemented catalytically, without consuming the additional N²-N queries required for the simulation. In the case of quantum circuits with quantum control of computational order, we prove a similar simulation result, but restricted to unitary input channels (hence non-universal). These results show the limitations of the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios.

item.title: Benchmarking superconducting quantum processors with percolating entanglement quality
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Introduced percolating entanglement quality (PEQ) to benchmark chip-wide graph states across different coupling topologies. Demonstrated on a 64-qubit square-lattice chip with defects, yielding a 52-qubit entanglement cluster and PEQ=0.42.

Grade 0.370 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Akinori Machino, Kazuhisa Ogawa, Takefumi Miyoshi, Hidehisa Shiomi, Shinichi Morisaka, Ryo Matsuda, Nilton F. G. Filho, Koichiro Ban, Takafumi Miyanaga, Keisuke Koike, Ryutaro Ohira, Toshi Sumida, Yoshinori Kurimoto, Yuuya Sugita, Yosuke Ito, Yasunari Suzuki, Peter A. Spring, Shiyu Wang, Hiroto Mukai, Arvind Mamgain, Shuhei Tamate, Yutaka Tabuchi, Yasunobu Nakamura, Makoto Negoro

Figure

Measured two-qubit conditional negativities across the 64-qubit square-lattice processor and the sorted distribution of edge negativities used to evaluate PEQ at the bond-percolation threshold.

Asks

How can chip-wide quantum processor entanglement be benchmarked on a common scale without ignoring individual coupling qualities or coupling topology differences?

Before

Cluster size and entanglement yield (EY) only count connected qubits; chips with full chip-spanning clusters (EY=1.00) show identical size scores despite widely differing link qualities.

But

Characterizes the prepared graph state rather than general circuit depth or gate fidelities; requires defining or numerically computing the infinite-lattice bond-percolation threshold for the processor topology.

Tools

native graph state preparation · conditional two-qubit state tomography · bond-percolation threshold · 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor

Abstract

The capability to create large entanglement resources is a key performance attribute of quantum processors, and the size of the resource is often used as a benchmark of processor scale. Recent graph-state experiments have reported entanglement clusters spanning entire chips with hundreds of qubits. However, cluster size alone does not capture the entanglement quality of individual couplings or differences in coupling topology. Here, we introduce percolating entanglement quality (PEQ), a topology-normalized benchmark based on conditional two-qubit negativity and a topology-specific bond-percolation threshold. As an experimental demonstration, we prepare a native graph state on a 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor with defects, identify a 52-qubit entanglement cluster, and evaluate the PEQ of the processor. Applying PEQ to previously reported chip-wide graph-state measurements on heavy-hex-lattice processors, we show that PEQ differs substantially among processors whose entanglement clusters span the entire chip. PEQ provides a single chip-wide score without selecting a best-performing qubit subset or path. This score allows processors with different coupling topologies to be compared on a common scale and can inform the design of coupling topologies for scalable chips.

item.arxave:abstract: The capability to create large entanglement resources is a key performance attribute of quantum processors, and the size of the resource is often used as a benchmark of processor scale. Recent graph-state experiments have reported entanglement clusters spanning entire chips with hundreds of qubits. However, cluster size alone does not capture the entanglement quality of individual couplings or differences in coupling topology. Here, we introduce percolating entanglement quality (PEQ), a topology-normalized benchmark based on conditional two-qubit negativity and a topology-specific bond-percolation threshold. As an experimental demonstration, we prepare a native graph state on a 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor with defects, identify a 52-qubit entanglement cluster, and evaluate the PEQ of the processor. Applying PEQ to previously reported chip-wide graph-state measurements on heavy-hex-lattice processors, we show that PEQ differs substantially among processors whose entanglement clusters span the entire chip. PEQ provides a single chip-wide score without selecting a best-performing qubit subset or path. This score allows processors with different coupling topologies to be compared on a common scale and can inform the design of coupling topologies for scalable chips.

item.title: Reference-Assisted Qutrit Control and Conditional One-Round Distillation in a Charge-4e Superconductor Model
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Formulates reference-assisted qutrit control for charge-4e superconductors under sector preservation and same-label covariance. Proves record probabilities are independent of reference state inside sector span SR=span⁡{|1⟩R,|2⟩R} for charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, yielding an accepted-run target infidelity bounded by eN+rν+rm+rγ.

Grade 0.370 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Junhao (Eigen), Wang

Asks

What operational conditions and error budgets govern reference-assisted qutrit control and conditional distillation using charge-4e parafermionic zero modes?

But

Requires sector-preserving instruments, same-label covariance, and accepted-run conditioning. Ignores native charge-4e extraction circuits, device thresholds, correlated Markov drift, and thermal quasiparticle leakage.

Tools

reference-assisted instrument formalism · ternary CSS [[11,1,5]]₃ decoder · classical flag refinement union bound · exact integer dynamic program

Abstract

We formulate a charge-4e parafermionic-vortex route to qutrit processing as a conditional theory with explicit operational assumptions. Sector preservation and same-label charge-conjugation covariance imply closure for every adaptive visible record. For charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, record probabilities are independent of the supported reference state; for arbitrary inputs, discarding the reference gives a population-weighted mixture of conjugate sector maps. We give a finite-depth stability bound for complete labelled instruments, including postselection and initial zero-sector contamination. A self-contained calculation reproduces the known dense single-qutrit closure of the registered Clifford-plus-Flip gate set. We also specify an abstract ternary CSS [[11,1,5]]₃ syndrome/recovery decoder: 243 classical representatives per CSS component correct all 3,609 Pauli errors of support weight at most two, and an exact integer dynamic program yields the full independent-Pauli logical enumerator. Its all-syndrome acceptance is distinct from the known 1/1728 ideal acceptance of one-round strange-state Golay distillation. An accepted-run target-infidelity budget and a synthetic parameter protocol expose the remaining noise assumptions. Native charge-4e syndrome extraction, material feasibility, a device threshold, and unconditional fault tolerance are not established.
